title: CMAs with Craig - August 5, 2026
summary: Hands-on CMA training session where Craig walks through two live property analyses: a two-story home in Murray (5646 South Crown Point Drive) and a rambler in Eagle Mountain (3827 East Pawnee Road). Covers the complete CMA workflow from tax record lookup through comp selection, adjustment methodology, and pricing recommendations. Key topics include how to handle properties with limited comps, when to stretch geographic boundaries, how to screen comps by lot size/year built/square footage, making upgrade adjustments, and communicating conservative ranges to sellers when interior condition is unknown.

broker_guidance.scenario: Property has never been on the MLS
broker_guidance.guidance: Start with tax records search to get basic stats (square footage, year built, lot size, bedroom/bath count). Then pull up Google Maps to assess location, streetscape, and neighboring properties before beginning comp selection.
broker_guidance.client_language: Let me pull the tax records first to get the baseline stats, then we'll see what comparable sales look like.

broker_guidance.scenario: Limited comps within tight geographic boundaries
broker_guidance.guidance: Be nuanced about stretching boundaries. In Murray, going too far east gets into much more expensive real estate near Wheeler Historic Farm. Going too far west or across the freeway changes the area character. North-south is often safer than east-west. Exclude condos, townhomes, and twins to narrow results. If still limited, stretch year built range or square footage tolerance cautiously.
broker_guidance.client_language: The comp selection is challenging here — the neighborhood is small and we may need to stretch boundaries carefully. East of 700 East gets into a different price tier entirely.

broker_guidance.guidance: Start at the bottom of the comp list and screen by lot size first — massive discrepancies get kicked out immediately. Land is the first discriminator. Then check garages (a third bay is at least a $20K difference), year built, and gross living area. Be willing to remove comps with multiple strikes against them (location, square footage, year built all off).
broker_guidance.client_language: I'm going to remove this one — the lot size is way off, and that's the first thing we screen for. Land value drives everything else.

broker_guidance.guidance: Active listings cannot be relied upon as sold comps. If a property has been sitting for 132+ days, it's evidently overpriced. Use active listings only to understand the ceiling or what NOT to do. Note days on market carefully — properties that sat through peak selling seasons (January-February) and still didn't sell are especially concerning.
broker_guidance.client_language: This active listing has been on the market 132 days — that tells us it's overpriced, not what the market actually supports.

broker_guidance.scenario: Making upgrade adjustments when interior is unknown
broker_guidance.guidance: When you haven't been inside the subject property, you can only take the analysis so far. Look at the exterior photos and Google Maps to estimate condition. If interior is unknown, give a conservative range (e.g., $700K-$800K) and tell the agent/seller it depends on upgrades. Go inside, take photos, then come back to finish adjustments. You don't have to give a final price on the first visit.
broker_guidance.client_language: Generally speaking, the analysis shows between $700K and $800K, but it really depends on upgrades and we need to see the inside. Let me come back and finish the analysis after I've toured the home.

broker_guidance.guidance: When comps are on the same road, same style (ramblers), similar lot sizes (0.14-0.20 acre), similar year built (2011-2018), and similar square footage (2300-2600), the analysis is extremely solid. You can confidently tell sellers: 'This analysis is crazy accurate.' Use this to push back against unrealistic seller expectations.
broker_guidance.client_language: This analysis is crazy accurate — the comps are on the same road, same style, same era, same size. There's no way around this number.

broker_guidance.scenario: Seller wants to list above what comps support
broker_guidance.guidance: Show them the analysis. The absolute highest the comps support is the top of the adjusted range. In the Eagle Mountain example, $505K was the absolute ceiling, with $495K being more realistic. If they insist on $549K, explain that the first 10 days on market have more energy than any other time, and overpricing means missing that window. Once energy is lost, even price drops may not bring it back.
broker_guidance.client_language: You could start there, but our analysis is crazy accurate. Five hundred would be fortunate. Five-oh-five is the absolute highest this analysis supports. The first 10 days on market has more energy than any other time — if you price too high, you lose that window and may never get it back.

broker_guidance.guidance: When a comp has an unfinished basement and the subject is 90% finished, give a bump for finishing. Craig suggests $35-40 per square foot for basement finish. In the Eagle Mountain example, a 5% finished basement got a $35K bump, and he considered raising it to $40/sq ft. Be consistent with your adjustment methodology across all comps.
broker_guidance.client_language: The comp has an unfinished basement — we're giving a $35-40K bump because our subject is 90% finished. That's a real value difference.

broker_guidance.guidance: When comparing kitchens, flooring, and bathrooms, estimate dollar values for the difference. A significantly updated kitchen might be a $30-40K advantage. Nicer bathrooms add value too. Backyards that back to open space might get a $10-15K bump. Solar panels that are paid off might get $10-20K depending on age and system cost. Make adjustments net — if interior is $40K better but exterior is $10K worse, net it to $30K.
broker_guidance.client_language: The kitchen and flooring on this comp are probably a $30-40K advantage. The yard is maybe $10K worse. So I'm netting that to about a $30K adjustment.

broker_guidance.scenario: Handling seller financing or unusual sales
broker_guidance.guidance: If a comp sold with seller financing, it's hard to keep in the analysis because the buyer probably overpaid. If it sold above list price with no concessions and used seller financing, it makes no sense as a comp and suggests a ceiling rather than support for value. Use caution with these and consider removing them.
broker_guidance.client_language: This one sold with seller financing above list price — that buyer probably overpaid. I'm not going to put much weight on this comp.

steps: Start with tax records search for baseline property stats
Pull up Google Maps to assess location, streetscape, and neighbors
Create new CMA and use the six status measurements (auto-sets 365 days back)
Set square footage range (typically +/- 500 sq ft from subject)
Set year built range (stretch cautiously if needed)
View map and assess geographic boundaries — be nuanced about which directions are safe to stretch
Exclude condos, townhomes, and twins if analyzing a single-family home
Screen comps starting with lot size — massive discrepancies get removed first
Check garages, year built, and gross living area for remaining comps
Remove comps with multiple strikes (location + size + year all off)
Make adjustments for upgrades, basement finish, lot size, and garage differences
If interior condition is unknown, give a conservative range and schedule a follow-up visit
For active listings, note days on market — long DOM suggests overpricing, not market value
Communicate the final range confidently, especially when comps are high-quality and local

objections.objection: Seller wants to list higher than comps support
objections.response: Show them the analysis with photos of the comps. Explain that the first 10 days on market has the most energy, and overpricing means missing that window permanently. Use specific comp addresses and adjusted values to make it concrete.

objections.objection: There aren't enough comps in the neighborhood
objections.response: Stretch boundaries carefully — north-south is often safer than east-west. Exclude non-similar property types. Consider going back further in time or slightly wider on square footage. Be transparent that the analysis is conservative when comp quality is lower.

objections.objection: The active listing down the street is priced higher
objections.response: Active listings don't determine value — only sold comps do. If an active listing has been sitting for 100+ days, it's overpriced, not evidence of market value. Use it as a cautionary example.

objections.objection: We haven't seen the inside yet
objections.response: That's fine — give a conservative range based on exterior and location, then schedule an interior visit. Take photos inside and come back to dial in the final number. You don't need to commit to a price on day one.

Speakers 2 and 3 are agent participants (Jana and Karen Ann). Craig demonstrates live CMA analysis on two real properties with specific addresses, dollar amounts, and adjustment methodologies. The chunk texts preserve Craig's exact phrasing and numerical examples.
operator_interpretation: No significant operator interpretation in this record. All broker_guidance items are directly supported by transcript excerpts. Craig's adjustment values ($20K for third garage bay, $35-40K for basement finish, $30-40K for kitchen upgrades, $10-15K for open space backyard) are his own stated methodologies from the transcript.
